title: Short thoughts from Vietnam about Big Data and Little Data
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton returns from a conference in Hanoi where a fellow speaker used PISA-style Big Data to argue that schooling must become more personalised. That prompted him to distinguish Big Data, which shows trends across countries and suits those who pull big policy levers, from Little Data, the localised evidence about a particular classroom or school. His point is that national scores cannot tell a teacher whether learning is happening in her own room. He presents the Looking for Learning grid as a Little Data tool that records new versus consolidated learning and whether students are treading water or drowning. That evidence is tied to seven questions about learning, teaching and school conditions. He closes by insisting both kinds of data are needed, but that agency for improvement lies with Little Data.
points: Large-scale data such as PISA describes national trends but is not designed to say anything about an individual classroom or school.
Little Data is not generalisable, and Skelton argues that this is exactly its value because it informs changes teachers and leaders can actually make.
Classroom observation of new versus consolidated learning and of knowledge, skills and understanding yields evidence for seven questions about whether learning is happening.
The same evidence can show what teachers do that helps or hinders learning and so shape a professional development programme that has real impact.
He frames this as complementary rather than oppositional: both data types together would improve the evidence base about learning.
quotes: What Big Data doesn’t show, can’t show, is what is happening in individual classrooms and individual schools. It isn’t designed for that.
Little Data gathers localised evidence about your particular situation. Little Data isn’t generalisable like Big Data but that is its strength to teachers, schools and organisational leaders.
We can’t make changes in our classroom or school based on Big Data. We need Little Data.

This Little Data is produced by small-scale research and reveals powerful insights about your classroom, your school and your context. These insights are not transferable to other classrooms or other schools but that is precisely its strength.
This is not an argument for Little Data against Big Data. We need both. In fact, if we had both working in tandem then the evidence base around learning would be hugely improved.
The Vietnam conference helped me see that my real interest is and has always been in Little Data about what is happening for children and students in my classroom and my school.
